## The data

This dataset lists 7,787 movies and TV shows that were on Netflix as of
early 2021. Each row is one title, with its type (movie or TV show),
director, cast, country, the date Netflix added it, its rating, its
length, the genres it is listed under, and a one-sentence description.
Almost every useful column is text. A movie's length is stored as a
string like "93 min", and a TV show's as "4 Seasons", so I use string
functions and regular expressions to turn that text into something I can
count and plot.

I look at three questions: how long movies run in different genres, what
the descriptions talk about, and how many seasons TV shows last.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

netflix <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2021/2021-04-20/netflix_titles.csv"
)
```

## How long are movies in each genre?

The `duration` column is text, so I pulled out the number with the
regular expression `^\d+(?= min)`. The `(?= min)` part is a
**lookahead**: it matches the digits only when " min" comes right after
them, without keeping " min" in the result. Each title can be listed
under several genres separated by commas, so I used the regular
expression `^[^,]+` to keep only the first genre listed.

```{r}
movies <- netflix |>
  filter(type == "Movie") |>
  mutate(
    minutes = as.numeric(str_extract(duration, "^\\d+(?= min)")),
    main_genre = str_extract(listed_in, "^[^,]+")
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(minutes))

top_genres <- movies |>
  count(main_genre, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 7) |>
  pull(main_genre)

movies |>
  filter(main_genre %in% top_genres) |>
  mutate(main_genre = fct_reorder(main_genre, minutes, .fun = median)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minutes, y = main_genre)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#E8D7B0", outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(
    x = "Movie length (minutes)",
    y = "First genre listed",
    title = "Dramas and action movies run longest; stand-up specials are shortest",
    subtitle = "Netflix movies in the seven most common genres"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Each box shows the middle half of movies in a genre, and the line inside
it is the median. Stand-up comedy specials are by far the shortest, with
a median of 65 minutes. Children's movies and documentaries come next at
about 86-87 minutes. Dramas and action and adventure movies have the
longest median, at 108 minutes. Every genre has long tails, with some
movies well over two hours.

## What do the descriptions talk about?

Next I searched each description for five common themes. I made the
text lowercase with `str_to_lower()` and used `str_detect()` with a
regular expression for each theme. `\b` marks a word boundary, so
`\bfamil(y|ies)\b` matches "family" and "families" but not "familiar",
and `\b(murder\w*|kill\w*)\b` catches "murder", "murderer", "killer",
and "killing."

```{r}
theme_patterns <- c(
  "Love"           = "\\blove\\b",
  "Murder/killing" = "\\b(murder\\w*|kill\\w*)\\b",
  "Family"         = "\\bfamil(y|ies)\\b",
  "Friendship"     = "\\bfriends?(hip)?\\b",
  "Secrets"        = "\\bsecrets?\\b"
)

themes <- netflix |>
  mutate(description = str_to_lower(description)) |>
  select(type, description) |>
  cross_join(tibble(theme = names(theme_patterns),
                    pattern = theme_patterns)) |>
  mutate(mentions = str_detect(description, pattern)) |>
  group_by(type, theme) |>
  summarize(share = mean(mentions), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(theme = fct_reorder(theme, share))

ggplot(themes, aes(x = share, y = theme, fill = type)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Movie" = "#1F4E4A", "TV Show" = "#C98A1B")) +
  labs(
    x = "Share of descriptions mentioning the theme",
    y = "Theme",
    fill = "Type of title",
    title = "TV show descriptions lean toward friends and family",
    subtitle = "Share of Netflix descriptions matching each theme"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Family and friendship are the most common of these themes, each showing
up in roughly 7-9% of descriptions. TV shows mention friendship (9.4%)
and family (8.8%) more often than movies do (7.2% and 7.5%), which makes
sense for series built around a recurring group of characters. Murder
and killing show up about equally in both, around 5.5-5.7%, and secrets
are the least common theme.

## How many seasons do TV shows last?

For TV shows, the `duration` column says something like "1 Season" or
"3 Seasons." The regular expression `^\d+(?= Seasons?)` uses another
lookahead to grab just the number, and the `s?` makes the final "s"
optional so it matches both "Season" and "Seasons." Then
`fct_lump_n()` groups every show with more than four seasons into an
"Other" category, which I relabel as "5 or more."

```{r}
netflix |>
  filter(type == "TV Show") |>
  mutate(
    seasons = str_extract(duration, "^\\d+(?= Seasons?)"),
    seasons = fct_lump_n(fct_infreq(seasons), n = 4,
                         other_level = "5 or more")
  ) |>
  count(seasons) |>
  mutate(percent = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 1)) |>
  rename(`Seasons on Netflix` = seasons, `TV shows` = n,
         `Percent` = percent) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Number of seasons for Netflix TV shows")
```

Two out of three TV shows on Netflix (67%) have only one season. Only
about 16% have two, and the share keeps dropping after that. One reason
is that Netflix often cancels shows after a single season, and another
is that many international series and limited series are written to be
one season long.
